EAST BETHANY, N.Y. (WIVB) -- Sharon Coyle had two goals when she bought Rolling Hills Asylum 17 years ago: save a piece of history and explore the paranormal.

“All I did was I wanted to save a place, and I wanted to talk to dead people, you know?” Coyle said. “And here it is.”

What started as a personal passion has grown into a destination known around the world, drawing visitors interested in the building’s history and reports of paranormal activity.

Rolling Hills Asylum opened in 1827 as the Genesee County Poorhouse. The institution provided shelter for people who needed help, including widows, orphans and people with physical or mental disabilities.

Coyle said she wanted to preserve the property at a time when historic buildings are disappearing.

“I wanted to rescue a historical property,” she said. “You know, they’re tearing down buildings left and right, statues left and right, and it’s such a part of American history, a poorhouse.”

For Coyle, preserving the building also means remembering the people who lived and died there. Over the years, she said, she has connected with relatives of former residents, learning more about their lives and the history of the property.

She said the people associated with the asylum have become like family.

“I mean, I feel very comfortable,” Coyle said. “I would say I was in here during the tornado. We lost all the power. I was in pitch black. Most people feel freaked out and I’m like, yeah, I’m here with my family. I’m going to be okay.”

Coyle said she sees the people who lived there as more than names in a historical record.

“They’re just humans. They’re someone’s mother, father and uncle, brother, sister, grandparent,” she said. “They’re just people like us and they’re really funny sometimes.”

Watch: Rolling Hills attracts the paranormal

Visitors can learn about that history through guided walking tours, which combine historical information with paranormal stories. The property also offers daytime, self-guided visits and ghost hunts, including overnight investigations for those looking for a more immersive experience.

Coyle said visitors do not need expensive equipment to get started.

“Come with your cell phone, just come for an experience,” she said. “You have a great camera on there, a great video camera, a great audio recorder and your personal senses. And that’s all you really need.”

She recalled one visitor who initially seemed skeptical but later reported hearing pots and pans crashing to the floor in the kitchen. When he went to investigate, he found nothing on the floor.

Coyle said she encourages visitors to examine potential evidence carefully rather than assume every unusual sound or image is paranormal.

“I want things to be authentic,” she said. “We don’t need to make stuff up.”

Beyond tours and investigations, Rolling Hills Asylum hosts special events, including psychic bingo, vendor fairs and horror movie nights. Coyle said the property’s 200th anniversary in 2027 will be another milestone, with a celebration planned and details still to be determined.

Despite the work involved in maintaining the property, Coyle said she is proud to have kept it going.

“It’s hard. It’s a lot of work. It’s my choice to be here,” she said. “But it is a lot of work. It’s like five full-time jobs.”

Still, hearing from visitors who have wanted to see the asylum for years reminds her why she took on the challenge.

“I think about how they feel,” Coyle said. “I get all emotional because it really, it blows me away.”

Coyle said visitors do not have to believe in ghosts to appreciate the property.

“The history is cool, the building’s cool,” she said. “You know, just come for that. And then if you end up having an experience, bonus for you.”

Rolling Hills Asylum will reach its 200th anniversary in 2027, giving Coyle another opportunity to honor the people who lived and died there while preserving a piece of local history.
